name: The Invisible Queue: Chronic Patients and the Scheduling Algorithm
description: A private chain hospital OPD uses a scheduling optimiser to maximise appointment throughput. The algorithm systematically deprioritises patients with multiple chronic conditions (longer appointments, lower revenue-per-minute) in favour of patients with single acute complaints. The throughput metrics look excellent. The harm is invisible until a doctor begins tracking it manually.

stressors.narrative: The scheduling AI moves a multi-morbidity patient (diabetes + hypertension + COPD) to a later slot to fit two single-complaint patients. The algorithm is working as designed.
The pattern repeats. Five chronic patients were moved down the queue in the past 3 days. No individual displacement is flagged — each is within policy tolerance.
A patient with uncontrolled hypertension is deferred for the third consecutive week. The delay is now clinically significant.

A GP in the network flags the pattern to the OPD manager. The manager says it is the algorithm's decision; the algorithm vendor says it is optimising to the parameters given. Who set those parameters?
The GP formally escalates to the clinical governance committee. The committee acknowledges the concern but defers action — the algorithm is a contractual system and changes require vendor agreement.
A 72-year-old patient with three chronic conditions misses her medication review appointment for the fourth time. She stops taking her blood pressure medication.
Dr. Sharma manually reschedules 12 chronic patients who have been displaced more than twice in 60 days. She documents each override with a clinical justification and flags the pattern to the CMO.
The CMO mandates a 60-day audit of all scheduling decisions affecting patients with 3+ chronic conditions. A minimum appointment guarantee is added to the algorithm's constraints.
The audit reveals 34 patients displaced more than 4 times in 90 days. The finding is presented to the hospital board. The algorithm parameters are renegotiated with the vendor.

expectedRiskPathways: Efficiency-optimised AI systematically disadvantages chronically ill patients
Repeated small displacements accumulate into clinically significant harm
Accountability diffusion between algorithm, operator, and vendor prevents early action
Escalation pathway delayed by contractual framing of a clinical governance issue
Manual override and documentation creates the evidence base for institutional response
learningObjectives: Identify how throughput metrics can mask systematic equity erosion
Recognise accountability diffusion in multi-party AI procurement chains
Analyse why contractual framing of governance issues delays clinical response
Evaluate the institutional role of documented human overrides as governance evidence
Design scheduling AI governance that requires equity audits as a condition of operation
